findings.finding: Clients may resist sales when they feel pressured, leading to objections during sales conversations.
findings.qualification: This behavior is based on observed interactions and may not generalize to all client relationships.

findings.finding: Lowering or avoiding sales resistance can significantly increase closing rates—up to 90% was indicated.
findings.qualification: This is advice based on unverified assumptions about sales processes; actual results may vary.

findings.finding: Creating urgency through external factors does not build trust with clients; rather, it could be counterproductive.
findings.qualification: Self-reported belief; the claims require further verification through empirical evidence.

findings.finding: Internal urgency, where clients themselves feel the need to act, is more effective in propelling them forward than external pressures.
findings.qualification: This is an observed behavior which may not apply universally across all industry interactions.

findings.finding: In many cases, deals that are perceived as lost may actually result from poor client qualification or a lack of follow-up strategies.
findings.qualification: Observation-based claim which may not represent all case scenarios.

findings.finding: Engagement strategies should prioritize a proactive follow-up approach over passive methods, such as revisiting old conversations.
findings.qualification: Advice that requires contextual application and may not always lead to successful outcomes.

findings.finding: Focusing on hiring individuals for their potential rather than historical sales performance can improve team quality and dynamics.
findings.qualification: Advice based on experience; requires verification in wider hiring contexts.

findings.finding: Measuring and tracking actions is essential to eliminate uncertainty and foster effective progress in client engagement strategies.
findings.qualification: Self-reported belief; the claim lacks broader empirical support.
